key_points.base: All three add a penalty to reduce variance. Ridge (L2) shrinks coefficients smoothly and keeps every
points: All three add a penalty that reduces variance
Ridge (L2) shrinks coefficients smoothly and keeps every feature
Lasso (L1) sets coefficients to zero, so it selects features
With correlated features lasso picks one arbitrarily; elastic net keeps the group
Standardize features before applying the penalty
Choose the penalty strength by cross-validation, time-aware for time data

points: Each split picks the feature and threshold that most reduce impurity
Impurity is Gini or entropy for classification, variance for regression
Splitting is greedy and never looks ahead
Unlimited depth fits noise until leaves are pure, so it overfits
Control it with max depth, minimum samples per leaf, pruning or ensembles
Trees predict piecewise constants and cannot extrapolate beyond the training range

key_points.base: Each tree trains on a bootstrap sample and considers a random subset of features at each split, so t
points: Each tree trains on a bootstrap sample of the rows
Each split considers a random subset of features, which decorrelates the trees
Averaging decorrelated trees reduces variance without adding much bias
Out-of-bag samples give a built-in validation estimate
Impurity importance is biased toward high-cardinality features and computed on training data
Use permutation importance on held-out data or SHAP; importance is not causation

key_points.base: All three are gradient-boosted trees, and with equal tuning they are usually within a small margin o
points: All three are gradient-boosted trees with similar accuracy when tuned equally
LightGBM grows leaf-wise with histograms: fast, but can overfit small data
XGBoost is the most widely deployed and documented, level-wise by default
CatBoost handles categorical features natively with ordered target statistics
With many categoricals, start with CatBoost
Compare all three on the same time-aware folds and tuning budget, including calibration

key_points.base: An SVM finds the separating boundary with the largest margin between classes; only the points neares
points: SVM finds the boundary with the largest margin between classes
Only the support vectors nearest the boundary define it
Kernels like RBF allow non-linear boundaries
C trades margin width against training errors; gamma sets how local the kernel is
Features must be standardized because it is distance-based
Good on small, high-dimensional data like text; slow on large data and scores are not probabilities

key_points.base: Linear regression minimizes squared error on every point. SVR defines a tube of width epsilon around
points: Linear regression penalizes squared error on every point
SVR ignores errors inside an epsilon tube around the fit
Errors outside the tube are penalized linearly, weighted by C
Only points on or outside the tube are support vectors, so it is robust to small noise and outliers
Needs scaled features and tuning of epsilon, C and gamma
Prefer it for small, smooth non-linear problems; otherwise regularized linear or boosting

key_points.base: k-NN stores the training data and predicts by taking the majority label (or the average) of the k cl
points: Predicts by majority vote or average of the k nearest training points
Small k is high variance; large k smooths toward the base rate; pick k by cross-validation
Features must be scaled and irrelevant ones removed
In high dimensions distances become similar, so neighbors lose meaning
Prediction is slow on large data without an index or approximate search

key_points.base: It multiplies per-feature likelihoods as if features were independent given the class. The assumptio
points: Assumes features are independent given the class and multiplies their likelihoods
Classification only needs the right class ranked first, which often survives the wrong assumption
Its probabilities are poorly calibrated; recalibrate before cost-based decisions
Trains in one pass and needs little data
Works well on high-dimensional sparse text, a strong baseline
Smoothing stops an unseen word from zeroing out a class

key_points.base: A coefficient is the change in log-odds of default for a one-unit increase in a feature with the oth
points: A coefficient is the change in log-odds per unit increase, others held fixed
Exponentiate a coefficient to get an odds ratio
Reading coefficients needs comparable scales and little collinearity
Check linearity in the log-odds; add splines, bins or interactions
Choose it when regulators need reasons, data is small, or the accuracy gap is within noise
Verify with a held-out comparison and calibration check

points: Isolation forest splits features at random; anomalies are isolated in fewer splits
Engineer behavioral features like amount versus the customer's norm and velocity
Set the threshold from review capacity, such as the top N per day
Unusual is not the same as fraud
Have analysts label the top of the ranking and measure precision
Feed the labels into a supervised model over time

points: Linear regression can predict negative counts and assumes constant variance
Use a Poisson GLM with a log link; effects are multiplicative on the rate
Check for overdispersion and use negative binomial if variance exceeds the mean
Add zero inflation when many customers have no claims
Use an exposure offset for customers observed for different periods
Gradient boosting with a Poisson objective is a flexible alternative

points: Alternates assigning points to the nearest center and moving centers to the mean
Finds a local optimum; use k-means++ and several restarts
Choose k with the elbow and silhouette, plus interpretability and stability
Fails on elongated shapes, very different cluster sizes and outliers
Needs scaled numeric features
DBSCAN or Gaussian mixtures are alternatives

key_points.base: DBSCAN grows clusters from dense neighborhoods: a point with at least min_samples neighbors within d
points: DBSCAN builds clusters from dense regions defined by eps and min_samples
Points in no dense region are labeled noise
Choose it for irregular shapes, unknown k, or when outliers matter
Struggles when clusters have very different densities
Struggles in high dimensions where distances lose meaning
Pick eps from a k-distance plot and scale features

key_points.base: Agglomerative clustering starts with each point alone and repeatedly merges the two closest clusters
points: Agglomerative clustering repeatedly merges the two closest clusters
The dendrogram records every merge and its distance
Linkage matters: single chains, complete is compact, average and Ward in between
Useful when the number of groups is unknown or structure is nested
Cut the tree at large gaps in merge height or where the business can act
Needs pairwise distances, so impractical beyond tens of thousands of points

key_points.base: k-means is a special case that assumes equal, round clusters and gives hard labels. A Gaussian mixtu
points: k-means assumes equal round clusters and gives hard labels
A Gaussian mixture lets clusters have their own mean, shape, size and weight
Soft assignments give each point a probability of membership
Fitted with expectation-maximization and can hit local optima
Choose the number of components with BIC or held-out likelihood
k-means is faster when clusters are round and hard labels are enough

points: Internal metrics like silhouette or Davies-Bouldin check compactness and separation
Those metrics favor round clusters and can mislead
Check stability by re-clustering on bootstrap samples or different seeds
Profile clusters on outcomes not used in clustering, like churn or revenue
A good segment can be described in a sentence and acted on

points: Start from the purpose: marketing, risk and service need different features
Engineer behavioral features, transform skewed ones and scale
For mixed data use Gower distance, k-prototypes, or PCA or embeddings first
Compare values of k on stability and interpretability
Explain segments by fitting a shallow decision tree on the labels
Refresh on a schedule and track membership drift

key_points.base: PCA finds orthogonal directions that capture the most variance and projects the data onto the first
points: PCA finds orthogonal directions of maximum variance and projects onto the top few
Used to compress correlated features, remove noise or visualize
Standardize first or large-scale features dominate
Choose components by cumulative explained variance, scree plot or downstream performance
Components are linear mixtures and hard to interpret
Poor fit for non-linear structure or when individual features must be explained

key_points.base: I'd say the plot is a good prompt but not proof. t-SNE (and UMAP to a lesser degree) preserves local
points: A t-SNE plot is a prompt, not proof
t-SNE preserves local neighborhoods but distorts global structure
Cluster sizes, gaps and positions in the plot are not reliable
Results change with perplexity and seed and can show clusters in pure noise
Re-run with several settings and cluster in the original or PCA space
Check stability and whether groups differ on outcomes the embedding never saw

key_points.base: With many more features than the data supports, I'd start with cheap filters: drop constants, near-d
points: Start with cheap filters: drop constants, near-duplicates and highly correlated features
Use embedded methods like lasso or tree importance to rank features
Wrapper methods like recursive elimination refine at higher cost
Do selection inside each cross-validation fold
Selecting on the full dataset first leaks labels and inflates the score
Regularized models or boosting often make heavy selection unnecessary

points: Ensembles help when models make different, uncorrelated errors
Stacking trains a meta-model on out-of-fold predictions

Try a simple average first; ship only if the gain beats maintenance and latency cost

points: Fix evaluation first: accuracy is meaningless; use precision-recall, PR AUC and cost
Class weights change the loss without changing the data
Undersampling discards data; oversampling duplicates rows
SMOTE interpolates synthetic points that can be unrealistic or overlap
Resample only inside the training fold, or validation leaks

points: Narrow the search to the hyperparameters that matter, like learning rate and depth
Use early stopping for the number of boosting rounds
Random search beats grid search because only a few hyperparameters matter
Bayesian optimization like Optuna is worth it when each run is expensive
